stances.claim: Intra-party disputes must first be resolved internally; if unresolved, the Comelec is legally mandated to determine the legitimate party officers, subject to Supreme Court review.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal pathway recital -- internal first, Comelec second, Court last.
stances.confidence: high -- straight statement of jurisprudential order

stances.claim: Legally, 'factions' do not exist -- only registered political parties do; candidates of the losing faction become independent candidates and lose party privileges.
stances.rhetorical_move: Categorical legal-purist correction of media usage.

stances.claim: Party endorsement carries substantial operational privileges -- copies of election returns, principal watchers, certificate-of-canvass copies, election-returns watermarking watchers, and higher per-voter spending allowance -- that materially advantage party-endorsed candidates.
stances.rhetorical_move: Quotes LDP v. Comelec verbatim to inventory the privileges; lets the doctrine speak for the strategic implication.
stances.confidence: very high -- direct quotation of binding precedent

stances.claim: Manny Pacquiao's best play if PDP-Laban's leadership is settled against him is coalition with the dominant minority (likely LP) or one of the six accredited major parties -- not running as independent.
stances.rhetorical_move: Strategic political-advice register grounded in the statutory privileges just inventoried.

one_paragraph_summary: Two PDP-Laban 'factions' -- one led by President Duterte as chair, Sec. Alfonso Cusi as president, and Melvin Matibag as secretary general; the other by Sen. Koko Pimentel as chair, Sen. Manny Pacquiao as president, and Ron Munsayac as executive director -- claim authority over the ruling party. CJ Panganiban lays out the jurisprudential pathway: internal resolution first, then Comelec adjudication (selecting between the two competing Sworn Information and Update Statements filed by the Aug. 15 deadline), then Supreme Court review. Crucially, he insists the law does not recognize 'factions' -- only registered political parties -- so candidates of the losing side become independent candidates. To explain why party affiliation matters operationally, he quotes at length from LDP v. Comelec (Feb. 24, 2004), inventorying the privileges that 'redound to the benefit of [a party's] candidates': election-return and certificate-of-canvass copies, principal watchers in precincts and at watermarking/printing sites, and -- most concretely -- higher per-voter spending allowances. From this doctrinal base he advances his strategic counsel: rather than running independent, Pacquiao should coalesce with the dominant minority (likely the Liberal Party, whose leader Leni Robredo has signaled openness) or one of the six accredited major parties. He closes with two real-time signals: Manila Mayor Isko Moreno has joined Aksyon Demokratiko (an accredited party, likely presidential prelude), and the rhetorical question of whether any accredited party would 'adopt Sen. Panfilo Lacson, the incorrigible nemesis of pork barrel.'
